title: Core localization polynomial equivalence
statement: Let A be a commutative ring, r a natural number, f : Fin r → A, and i : Fin r. Write I = (∑ j, f(j)X_j - 1), B = A[X_j : j : Fin r]/I [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], Af = A localized at f(i), and Bf = B localized at the image of f(i) [def-weil-ring-localization-away]. Equip Bf with its induced Af-algebra structure [lem-weil-pbc-localization-away-universal-property]. Then there exists an Af-algebra equivalence Af[Y_j : j ≠ i] ≃ Bf whose forward homomorphism is evaluation at the localized classes x_j of X_j, and whose inverse sends x_j to Y_j for every j ≠ i.

source.place: Smoothing Ring Maps, proof of Lemma Tag 07EU (lemma-final-solve): 'B_{f_i} is smooth over A_{f_i}. Details omitted.' (the isomorphism is the omitted detail)

proof.text: Use polynomial evaluation for the forward map. For the inverse, send X_i to f(i)⁻¹(1−∑ j ≠ i f(j)Y_j) and X_j to Y_j otherwise. The relation evaluates to zero; factor through the quotient, then extend through localization since f(i) maps to a unit. The extension respects Af coefficients by uniqueness of localization. The two composites fix all generators, using the relation for X_i, and are identities by polynomial, quotient and localization uniqueness.

blueprint_update.statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $r\ge1$, $f_1,\dots,f_r\in A$ and $1\le i\le r$. Put
$$
B=A[X_1,\dots,X_r]\Big/\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^rf_jX_j-1\Bigr),
$$
let $A_{f_i}=A[1/f_i]$, and let $B_{f_i}$ be the localization of $B$ at the image of $f_i$,
an $A_{f_i}$-algebra via the map induced by $A\to B$. Write $x_j\in B_{f_i}$ for the image of
$X_j$. Then there is an isomorphism of $A_{f_i}$-algebras
$$
\varphi\colon A_{f_i}[Y_j : j\ne i]\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }B_{f_i}
$$
from the polynomial ring in the $r-1$ variables $Y_j$, $j\ne i$, such that $\varphi$ is the
evaluation homomorphism $Y_j\mapsto x_j$ $(j\ne i)$ and $\varphi^{-1}(x_j)=Y_j$ for every
$j\ne i$.

proof.text:
Let $\varphi$ be the $A_{f_i}$-algebra homomorphism with $\varphi(Y_j)=x_j$ for $j\ne i$. For
the inverse, let $\psi_0\colon A[X_1,\dots,X_r]\to A_{f_i}[Y_j : j\ne i]$ be the $A$-algebra
homomorphism with $\psi_0(X_i)=f_i^{-1}\bigl(1-\sum_{j\ne i}f_jY_j\bigr)$ and
$\psi_0(X_j)=Y_j$ for $j\ne i$. It sends $\sum_jf_jX_j-1$ to $0$, so it factors through $B$,
and since $f_i$ maps to a unit it extends to $\psi\colon B_{f_i}\to A_{f_i}[Y_j : j\ne i]$.
By the universal property of localization, $\psi$ is $A_{f_i}$-linear. The two composites
$\psi\circ\varphi$ and $\varphi\circ\psi$ fix all generators (for $x_i$ use the relation
$f_ix_i=1-\sum_{j\ne i}f_jx_j$ in $B_{f_i}$). An algebra homomorphism out of a polynomial
ring, a quotient of it, or a localization of such a quotient is determined by its values on
the generators, so both composites are identities. Hence $\varphi$ is an isomorphism with
inverse $\psi$, and $\varphi^{-1}(x_j)=\psi(x_j)=Y_j$ for $j\ne i$.
